title: Cardiometabolic and molecular adaptations to 6-month intermittent fasting in middle-aged men and women with overweight: secondary outcomes of a randomized controlled trial

paper_content.abstract: Intermittent fasting (IF) has gained attention as a potential intervention for cardiometabolic health, though its long-term effects remain unclear. In this randomized clinical trial, we assessed the impact of 6 months of IF on body composition, cardiovascular risk factors, and related molecular pathways in middle-aged (30-65 years) men and women with overweight (BMI 24.8–35 kg/m²). In this trial, 41 participants were randomized to either an intermittent fasting (IF) intervention or to maintain their habitual diet. The primary outcome (circulating CRP concentration) was previously reported; here, we present exploratory analyses focusing on metabolomic and transcriptomic responses. IF led to an 8% reduction in body weight, a 16% decrease in body fat, and significant improvements in lipid profile, including substantial reductions in plasma LDL-cholesterol, non-HDL-cholesterol, and triglycerides (p = 0.001). However, no significant changes were observed in other cardiometabolic risk factors. To investigate the underlying molecular mechanisms, we performed untargeted plasma metabolomics and transcriptomic analysis of colon mucosa biopsies. Significant multi-omic changes were identified, particularly in lipid metabolism, bile acid signaling, and enteroendocrine regulation. Notably, there was a downregulation of transcripts related to glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) and related enteroendocrine hormones. Correlation analysis highlighted key molecular pathways, with PPAR-α and B-cell-mediated immune processes significantly associated with changes in non-HDL cholesterol. Our findings extend the understanding of IF in humans beyond weight loss, providing key mechanistic insights to inform targeted therapies for improving cardiometabolic health. ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01964118
paper_content.introduction:
Cardiovascular disease remains a global health concern, contributing to substantial morbidity, disability, mortality, and escalating healthcare costs. Men and women with optimal cardiometabolic health at age 50 have a 13-fold lower risk of developing cardiovascular disease compared to those with two or more abnormal risk factors, even accounting for longer life expectancy. Previous research, both observational and randomized trials, has demonstrated that daily calorie restriction with a balanced intake of nutrient-rich foods, particularly those high in vegetable fiber and vitamins, causes substantial improvements in multiple major cardiometabolic risk factors. These effects have been observed even in lean and slightly overweight young adults. However, adhering to daily calorie restriction can be challenging, highlighting the need for easier-to-implement strategies. Intermittent fasting (IF) has gained popularity for weight loss, allowing individuals to follow their regular diet on non-fasting days. However, despite promising results in rodents, clinical trials on IF in adults with overweight and obesity have shown mixed effects on cardiometabolic indicators, with one trial even reporting increased plasma LDL-cholesterol levels.

The present randomized clinical trial was designed to assess whether sustained weight loss achieved through long-term IF can replicate the cardiometabolic benefits observed with chronic calorie restriction with optimal nutrient intake in men and women with overweight and obesity, while also exploring the underlying molecular mechanisms. The primary outcome (circulating CRP concentration) was previously reported, with no significant changes in CRP. Here, we present secondary analyses focusing on metabolomic and transcriptomic responses. A key aspect of this trial is the multi-omic analysis of colon mucosa biopsies, aimed at understanding how IF impacts lipid metabolism in the colon and cardiometabolic health. The colon plays a critical role in nutrient absorption, cholesterol metabolism, and bile acid recycling – key processes in maintaining metabolic homeostasis. Molecular analysis of colon tissue can elucidate how IF modulates lipid absorption, bile acid signaling, and inflammatory responses, all of which are essential for regulating cholesterol, triglycerides, and overall cardiovascular health. Additionally, the colon’s interaction with the gut microbiota and its involvement in systemic inflammation and immune modulation make it a critical site for understanding the broader metabolic effects of IF. By uncovering these mechanisms, this study aims to provide insights into how IF influences cardiometabolic outcomes, potentially informing targeted dietary, pharmacological, and personalized metabolic strategies.

In this study, we show that six months of IF significantly reduces body weight and adiposity, leading to favourable changes in lipid profiles, but without affecting other major cardiovascular risk factors. Notably, baseline levels of PPAR-α–related transcripts predicted the magnitude of lipid improvements. Integrated multi-omic profiling of plasma and colonic mucosa revealed downregulation of GLP-1–associated enteroendocrine signalling, including reduced glucagon (GCG) and peptide YY (PYY) expression, alongside modulation of B-cell pathways. These findings extend current understanding of IF beyond weight loss, providing mechanistic insights into its cardiometabolic benefits.

Multi-omicchangesinresponsetoIF

In contrast, 393 entities were downregulated, including 387 genes and 6 metabolites (lactulose, 2-hydroxybutanoic acid, 3 unannotated metabolites, and the protein IL-6). The biological knowledge analysis of significantly changed entities was conducted using CompBio v2.6, resulting in two distinct maps representing biological processes – one for upregulated processes and another for downregulated processes. No biological themes met the significance threshold for upregulated entities (Source Data). In contrast, more than 30 interconnected biological themes were significant for downregulated entities. Full maps, along with a comprehensive list of themes, associated genes, and concepts, are available in the supplementary material (Supplementary Fig. 4). Figure 1 highlights the key findings related to the downregulated entities associated with 6-month IF. Notably, enteroendocrine signaling emerged as a central theme, connecting various sub-themes such as the synthesis and secretion of glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), a hormone crucial for appetite regulation and insulin secretion. Genes most strongly enriched in this theme, such as glucagon (GCG) and peptide YY (PYY), are highlighted in the red panel (Fig. 1). Additionally, the metabolite lactulose was mapped to this theme, showing a modest enrichment score of 7.11.

Another significantly downregulated theme, Pituitary Adenylate Cyclase-Activating Polypeptide (PACAP) receptor activity, shown in blue (Fig. 1), was strongly interconnected with the GLP-1 theme. Key genes within this theme, such as vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) and adenylate cyclase activating polypeptide 1 (ADCYAP1), exhibited the greatest enrichment scores. The two themes shared 20 genes, many of which are involved in the synthesis, secretion, and proteolytic cleavage of endocrine peptides. These genes include not only PYY and GCG, but also pancreatic polypeptide (PPY), somatostatin (SST), and others like ISL LIM homeobox 1 (ISL1), carboxypeptidase E (CPE), and secretagogin (SCGN). Shared genes with the greatest contributions are visualized in the map. Figure 1 also presents a concept map for the GLP-1 theme, illustrating the interconnected terms and their relationships. On one side, terms related to appetite, hunger, and satiety are linked to GLP-1, while insulin and islet function are positioned on the opposite side, with GLP-1 at the center. Figure 1b (panel below the map) provides a schematic diagram that depicts the relationship between IF and enteroendocrine function, as revealed by the multi-omics analysis.

Correlationanalysisbetweenmulti-omicdataandlipid/lipoproteinchanges
Statisticallysignificantchangesinmultiplelipidandlipoproteinparameterswereobservedbetweenbaselineand6months,asdetailedinTable2.Toexplorethemolecularpathwayspotentiallylinkedtothese lipid-related changes, we performed correlation analysis between changes in entity expression/abundance and non-HDL cholesterol (non-HDL-C) levels over the 6-month IF period. Using non-parametric Spearman correlation analysis (r≥0.4 with p value<1.0E-9), we identified 280 entities positively correlated and 329 entities negatively correlated with plasma non-HDL-C levels. The CompBio knowledge map for entities positively correlated with non-HDL-C (Fig. 2) revealed a broad range of interconnected processes, including lipid metabolism regulation by PPAR alpha (PPAR-α), protein lipidation in autophagosome assembly, brush border-enterocyte transports, and unmethylated CpG binding. Genes showing the greatest enrichment scores within these themes included peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor PPAR-α (r=0.55, p=2.22E-14), sequestome 1 SQSTM1 (r=0.41, p=3.16E-10), myosin 7b MYO7B (r=0.46, p=1.08E-11), and methyl CpG binding domain 1 MBD1 (r=0.41, p=2.89E-10).

In contrast, the CompBio knowledge map for entities negatively correlated with non-HDL-C (Fig. 3) unveiled a significant cluster of seventeen B-cell and immune-based themes, including isotype switching, dendritic cells in Th1 and Th2 regulation, and CCR5 chemokine receptor binding. Highly enriched genes within these themes included CD79a (r=−0.51 p=3.05E-13), Bruton tyrosine kinase BTK (r=−0.52, p1.35E-13), complement receptor CR1 (r=−0.4, p=4.55E-10), Fcepsilon receptor 1 FCER2 (r=−0.42, p=9.89E-11), immunoglobulin heavy constant alpha 1 IGHA1 (r=−0.43, p=6.37E-11) and immunoglobulin heavy constant gamma 1 IGHG1 (r=−0.41, p=2.02E-10). Full maps, along with a complete list of the identified biological themes and associated genes, are provided (Source Data, Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6). Further analysis of the relationship between B-cell gene expression and changes in non-HDL-C revealed interesting dynamics. A median B-cell profile, constructed from seven marker genes (i.e., CD23, CD79A, CD79B, CD19, NUGGC, BTK, and CD27), showed a negative correlation with the non-HDL-C ratio (r=−0.56, p=0.0021). This suggests that as the non-HDL-C ratio decreases during IF, the B-cell profile tends to increase for most participants (Fig. 3). However, a small subset of individuals exhibited an inverse correlation, suggesting differential immune responses to lipid changes induced by IF. Interestingly, maps generated for triglyceride changes exhibited similar themes to those observed for non-HDL-C, though these did not reach statistical significance. As a result, all comparisons were made using non-HDL-C as the primary lipid parameter of interest.

EffectofbaselineprofileonIF-inducedmulti-omicchangesinnon-HDLcholesterol
Variabilityinnon-HDL-Clevelchangeswasobservedamongparticipants overthe6-monthIFintervention(SupplementaryFig.7).Toexplorethemolecularbasisofthisvariability,wecorrelatedbaselinegeneexpressionwithchangesinnon-HDL-Clevels(6-monthtobaselineratio).Usingnon-parametricSpearmancorrelationanalysis(r≥0.4withpvalue<1.0E-9), we identified 347 genes positively correlated and 535 negatively correlated with non-HDL-C. These genes underwent analysis using CompBio v2.6 for biological knowledge mapping, revealing significant insights, particularly in the negatively correlated map. Three main clusters emerged, linked to adherens junctions and signaling, PKA signaling and cargo transport, and epigenetic modulation (Fig. 4). Full maps, along with a comprehensive list of identified biological themes and associated genes, are available (Source Data, Supplementary Fig. 8). At the core of these clusters is the regulation of lipid metabolism by the PPAR-α theme, comprising 42 entities and 32 concepts. Within each cluster, graph panels highlight genes with the strongest enrichment for representative themes. As expected, the PPAR-α theme demonstrated strong enrichment for PPAR-α (r=−0.56, p=1.13E-14) and UCP3 (r=−0.41, p=2.76E-10). Given the robust correlation between baseline PPAR-α expression and non-HDL cholesterol changes, we performed a more detailed investigation into individual participant-level alterations. Figure 4 shows the relationship between each participant’s baseline PPAR-α expression (log2 CPM) and their corresponding non-HDL-C ratio (6-month to baseline). Remarkably, as baseline PPAR-α expression increased during IF, the non-HDL cholesterol ratio decreased, indicating a reduction in non-HDL-C levels over the 6 months compared to baseline. The summary of findings is presented in Fig. 5.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The study by Barve highlights body weight and adiposity, metabolomic, and molecular adaptations from IF despite lack of physiological changes in cardiometabolic function. The study is well written and rich in novel data.
The major limitation is that age and sex are not taken into consideration in the analysis. I would like to know if either is a significant variable. Moreover, it is unclear if and what % of women are pre or post-menopause. IF in women may lead to a substantially different responses compared to men due to changes in cycling hormones.
Is the untargetted metabolomics data deposited?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The study concept was novel and manuscript was well written. However, there are several concerns regarding statistics analysis:
1.Based upon the study protocol, the sample size calculation was based on inflammatory marker (C-reactive protein): the sample size of N=25 for each group seems calculated using two-tailed t-test (power=0.8,alpha error rate 0.05). However, the final sample size that can be used for outcomes changes (6 month-baseline) was only 21 for A group (IF) and 20 for B group (control). It means the final analysis was underpowered.
2.As in the protocol, the primary objective of this study is to determine whether or not IF reduces the level of chronic inflammation as evidenced by a decrease in high sensitive C-reactive protein (hsCRP), as the main outcome measure. In addition, the sample size calculation was based upon hsCRP as well. But the manuscript seemed to have little discussion about hsCRP results (although result not statistically significant).
3.In table 1, the third column is the group A+D (sample size was noted as 41). Based on line 90-91, 20 out of 22 participants from control group B crossed over to IF for the second 6 months (group D). Then 5% dropout from group D and n=15 was analyzed at month 12. Since both baseline and follow-up were needed to calculate the delta change, therefore, the actually sample size would be only 15 in D group?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Intermittent fasting (IF) exerts beneficial effects in experimental models, whose application for clinical therapy is one of the emerging interests. In this manuscript, the authors designed RCT trial to evaluate the physiological impact of 6-month IF. Participants with overweight (BMI 24.8–35 kg/m²) at middle-aged (30-65 years) were randomly assigned to IF or usual diet. The populations in IF displayed reduction in body weight and body fat, 8% and 16% respectively, accompanied with improvements in lipid profile, including substantial reductions in plasma LDL, non-HDL-cholesterol, and triglycerides. By multi-omics approach, including untargeted plasma metabolomics and transcriptomic analysis of colon mucosa biopsies, the authors identified the significant changed profiles in lipid metabolism, bile acid signaling, glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1), and enteroendocrine hormones. Moreover, non-HDL cholesterol significantly correlated with PPAR-α and B-cell-mediated immune processes. These finding disclosed the novel aspects of human IF, beyond weight loss. However, several flaws in the study make the reviewer difficult to interpret the data properly. The reviewer shows several concerns, which should be resolved. Otherwise, the manuscript is not acceptable for the journal.

## Abstract

Intermittent fasting (IF) has gained attention as a potential intervention for cardiometabolic health, though its long-term effects remain unclear. In this randomized clinical trial, we assessed the impact of 6 months of IF on body composition, cardiovascular risk factors, and related molecular pathways in middle-aged (30-65 years) men and women with overweight (BMI 24.8–35 kg/m²). In this trial, 41 participants were randomized to either an intermittent fasting (IF) intervention or to maintain their habitual diet. The primary outcome (circulating CRP concentration) was previously reported; here, we present exploratory analyses focusing on metabolomic and transcriptomic responses. IF led to an 8% reduction in body weight, a 16% decrease in body fat, and significant improvements in lipid profile, including substantial reductions in plasma LDL-cholesterol, non-HDL-cholesterol, and triglycerides (p = 0.001). However, no significant changes were observed in other cardiometabolic risk factors. To investigate the underlying molecular mechanisms, we performed untargeted plasma metabolomics and transcriptomic analysis of colon mucosa biopsies. Significant multi-omic changes were identified, particularly in lipid metabolism, bile acid signaling, and enteroendocrine regulation. Notably, there was a downregulation of transcripts related to glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) and related enteroendocrine hormones. Correlation analysis highlighted key molecular pathways, with PPAR-α and B-cell-mediated immune processes significantly associated with changes in non-HDL cholesterol. Our findings extend the understanding of IF in humans beyond weight loss, providing key mechanistic insights to inform targeted therapies for improving cardiometabolic health. ## Introduction

Cardiovascular disease remains a global health concern, contributing to substantial morbidity, disability, mortality, and escalating healthcare costs. Men and women with optimal cardiometabolic health at age 50 have a 13-fold lower risk of developing cardiovascular disease compared to those with two or more abnormal risk factors, even accounting for longer life expectancy. Previous research, both observational and randomized trials, has demonstrated that daily calorie restriction with a balanced intake of nutrient-rich foods, particularly those high in vegetable fiber and vitamins, causes substantial improvements in multiple major cardiometabolic risk factors. These effects have been observed even in lean and slightly overweight young adults. However, adhering to daily calorie restriction can be challenging, highlighting the need for easier-to-implement strategies. Intermittent fasting (IF) has gained popularity for weight loss, allowing individuals to follow their regular diet on non-fasting days. However, despite promising results in rodents, clinical trials on IF in adults with overweight and obesity have shown mixed effects on cardiometabolic indicators, with one trial even reporting increased plasma LDL-cholesterol levels.

The present randomized clinical trial was designed to assess whether sustained weight loss achieved through long-term IF can replicate the cardiometabolic benefits observed with chronic calorie restriction with optimal nutrient intake in men and women with overweight and obesity, while also exploring the underlying molecular mechanisms. The primary outcome (circulating CRP concentration) was previously reported, with no significant changes in CRP. Here, we present secondary analyses focusing on metabolomic and transcriptomic responses. A key aspect of this trial is the multi-omic analysis of colon mucosa biopsies, aimed at understanding how IF impacts lipid metabolism in the colon and cardiometabolic health. The colon plays a critical role in nutrient absorption, cholesterol metabolism, and bile acid recycling – key processes in maintaining metabolic homeostasis. Molecular analysis of colon tissue can elucidate how IF modulates lipid absorption, bile acid signaling, and inflammatory responses, all of which are essential for regulating cholesterol, triglycerides, and overall cardiovascular health. Additionally, the colon’s interaction with the gut microbiota and its involvement in systemic inflammation and immune modulation make it a critical site for understanding the broader metabolic effects of IF. By uncovering these mechanisms, this study aims to provide insights into how IF influences cardiometabolic outcomes, potentially informing targeted dietary, pharmacological, and personalized metabolic strategies.

In this study, we show that six months of IF significantly reduces body weight and adiposity, leading to favourable changes in lipid profiles, but without affecting other major cardiovascular risk factors. Notably, baseline levels of PPAR-α–related transcripts predicted the magnitude of lipid improvements. Integrated multi-omic profiling of plasma and colonic mucosa revealed downregulation of GLP-1–associated enteroendocrine signalling, including reduced glucagon (GCG) and peptide YY (PYY) expression, alongside modulation of B-cell pathways. These findings extend current understanding of IF beyond weight loss, providing mechanistic insights into its cardiometabolic benefits.

### Reviewer 1

The study by Barve highlights body weight and adiposity, metabolomic, and molecular adaptations from IF despite lack of physiological changes in cardiometabolic function. The study is well written and rich in novel data.
The major limitation is that age and sex are not taken into consideration in the analysis. I would like to know if either is a significant variable. Moreover, it is unclear if and what % of women are pre or post-menopause. IF in women may lead to a substantially different responses compared to men due to changes in cycling hormones.
Is the untargetted metabolomics data deposited?

### Reviewer 2

The study concept was novel and manuscript was well written. However, there are several concerns regarding statistics analysis:
1.Based upon the study protocol, the sample size calculation was based on inflammatory marker (C-reactive protein): the sample size of N=25 for each group seems calculated using two-tailed t-test (power=0.8,alpha error rate 0.05). Intermittent fasting (IF) exerts beneficial effects in experimental models, whose application for clinical therapy is one of the emerging interests. In this randomized clinical trial, we assessed the impact of 6 months of IF on body composition, cardiovascular risk factors, and related molecular pathways in middle-aged (30-65 years) men and women with overweight (BMI 24.8–35 kg/m²). In this trial, 41 participants were randomized to either an intermittent fasting (IF) intervention or to maintain their habitual diet. The primary outcome (circulating CRP concentration) was previously reported; here, we present exploratory analyses focusing on metabolomic and transcriptomic responses. IF led to an 8% reduction in body weight, a 16% decrease in body fat, and significant improvements in lipid profile, including substantial reductions in plasma LDL-cholesterol, non-HDL-cholesterol, and triglycerides (p = 0.001). However, no significant changes were observed in other cardiometabolic risk factors. To investigate the underlying molecular mechanisms, we performed untargeted plasma metabolomics and transcriptomic analysis of colon mucosa biopsies. Significant multi-omic changes were identified, particularly in lipid metabolism, bile acid signaling, and enteroendocrine regulation. Notably, there was a downregulation of transcripts related to glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) and related enteroendocrine hormones. Correlation analysis highlighted key molecular pathways, with PPAR-α and B-cell-mediated immune processes significantly associated with changes in non-HDL cholesterol. Our findings extend the understanding of IF in humans beyond weight loss, providing key mechanistic insights to inform targeted therapies for improving cardiometabolic health. ## Introduction

Cardiovascular disease remains a global health concern, contributing to substantial morbidity, disability, mortality, and escalating healthcare costs. Men and women with optimal cardiometabolic health at age 50 have a 13-fold lower risk of developing cardiovascular disease compared to those with two or more abnormal risk factors, even accounting for longer life expectancy. Previous research, both observational and randomized trials, has demonstrated that daily calorie restriction with a balanced intake of nutrient-rich foods, particularly those high in vegetable fiber and vitamins, causes substantial improvements in multiple major cardiometabolic risk factors. These effects have been observed even in lean and slightly overweight young adults. However, adhering to daily calorie restriction can be challenging, highlighting the need for easier-to-implement strategies. Intermittent fasting (IF) has gained popularity for weight loss, allowing individuals to follow their regular diet on non-fasting days. However, despite promising results in rodents, clinical trials on IF in adults with overweight and obesity have shown mixed effects on cardiometabolic indicators, with one trial even reporting increased plasma LDL-cholesterol levels.

The present randomized clinical trial was designed to assess whether sustained weight loss achieved through long-term IF can replicate the cardiometabolic benefits observed with chronic calorie restriction with optimal nutrient intake in men and women with overweight and obesity, while also exploring the underlying molecular mechanisms. The primary outcome (circulating CRP concentration) was previously reported, with no significant changes in CRP. Here, we present secondary analyses focusing on metabolomic and transcriptomic responses. A key aspect of this trial is the multi-omic analysis of colon mucosa biopsies, aimed at understanding how IF impacts lipid metabolism in the colon and cardiometabolic health. The colon plays a critical role in nutrient absorption, cholesterol metabolism, and bile acid recycling – key processes in maintaining metabolic homeostasis. Molecular analysis of colon tissue can elucidate how IF modulates lipid absorption, bile acid signaling, and inflammatory responses, all of which are essential for regulating cholesterol, triglycerides, and overall cardiovascular health. Additionally, the colon’s interaction with the gut microbiota and its involvement in systemic inflammation and immune modulation make it a critical site for understanding the broader metabolic effects of IF. By uncovering these mechanisms, this study aims to provide insights into how IF influences cardiometabolic outcomes, potentially informing targeted dietary, pharmacological, and personalized metabolic strategies.

In this study, we show that six months of IF significantly reduces body weight and adiposity, leading to favourable changes in lipid profiles, but without affecting other major cardiovascular risk factors. Notably, baseline levels of PPAR-α–related transcripts predicted the magnitude of lipid improvements. Integrated multi-omic profiling of plasma and colonic mucosa revealed downregulation of GLP-1–associated enteroendocrine signalling, including reduced glucagon (GCG) and peptide YY (PYY) expression, alongside modulation of B-cell pathways. These findings extend current understanding of IF beyond weight loss, providing mechanistic insights into its cardiometabolic benefits.

Cardiovascular disease remains a global health concern, contributing to substantial morbidity, disability, mortality, and escalating healthcare costs. Men and women with optimal cardiometabolic health at age 50 have a 13-fold lower risk of developing cardiovascular disease compared to those with two or more abnormal risk factors, even accounting for longer life expectancy. Previous research, both observational and randomized trials, has demonstrated that daily calorie restriction with a balanced intake of nutrient-rich foods, particularly those high in vegetable fiber and vitamins, causes substantial improvements in multiple major cardiometabolic risk factors. These effects have been observed even in lean and slightly overweight young adults. However, adhering to daily calorie restriction can be challenging, highlighting the need for easier-to-implement strategies. Intermittent fasting (IF) has gained popularity for weight loss, allowing individuals to follow their regular diet on non-fasting days. However, despite promising results in rodents, clinical trials on IF in adults with overweight and obesity have shown mixed effects on cardiometabolic indicators, with one trial even reporting increased plasma LDL-cholesterol levels.

The present randomized clinical trial was designed to assess whether sustained weight loss achieved through long-term IF can replicate the cardiometabolic benefits observed with chronic calorie restriction with optimal nutrient intake in men and women with overweight and obesity, while also exploring the underlying molecular mechanisms. Additionally, the colon’s interaction with the gut microbiota and its involvement in systemic inflammation and immune modulation make it a critical site for understanding the broader metabolic effects of IF. These findings extend current understanding of IF beyond weight loss, providing mechanistic insights into its cardiometabolic benefits.
